profilePeriod: 1977–1981 presidency for institutional/economic policy; explicitly dated 1996–2015 post-presidential statements for later peace, civil-rights, faith and science positions.
scopeNote: Answers are editorial simulations of documented political principles, not a questionnaire completed by the person. Brazil-specific statements are interpreted in the analogous home-country context. Modern hypothetical technologies require inference.

sources.title: Department of Education proposal
sources.evidence: Carter assigned primary educational responsibility to states and local governments while proposing a federal cabinet department for equal access, research and coordination.

sources.title: Elementary and Secondary Education Message
sources.evidence: Proposed strengthening bilingual schooling, with learning English the overriding goal and flexible use of first languages and culturally sensitive methods.

sources.title: Indian Education Programs
sources.evidence: Reorganization explicitly preserved tribal self-determination, federal trust obligations and tribal/parental participation.

sources.title: Nobel Peace Prize Lecture
sources.evidence: Defended constitutional democracy, human rights, UN collective security and peaceful settlement. Described necessary military readiness and diplomacy together, rejecting unilateral military predominance.

sources.title: A Cruel and Unusual Record
sources.evidence: Condemned indefinite terrorist detention, warrantless wiretapping, electronic data mining, torture and targeted killings. Defended presumption of innocence and judicial/congressional oversight.

sources.title: Drug Abuse Remarks
sources.evidence: Favored removing federal criminal penalties for possession of up to one ounce of marijuana, while distinguishing decriminalization from legalization and preserving state choices.

sources.title: Undocumented Aliens Message
sources.evidence: Proposed status regularization for established residents alongside employer sanctions, border enforcement and removal of recent unlawful entrants. Explicitly prohibited discriminatory implementation and rejected a national identity card.

sources.title: Carter and Human Rights
sources.evidence: State Department history documents tying military/economic assistance to recipient human rights and diplomatic pressure, with flexible rather than uniform enforcement.

sources.title: Presidency of Jimmy Carter: foreign policy overview
sources.evidence: Documents 1980 warning that external domination of the Persian Gulf would be resisted, including military force, alongside earlier human-rights diplomacy.

sources.title: National Health Plan
sources.evidence: Proposed expanded low-income coverage, compulsory employer catastrophic coverage and unified federal Healthcare administration. Kept competing HMOs/private claims administrators, imposed cost controls and delayed new expenditure for budget reasons.

sources.title: Airline Deregulation Act signing
sources.evidence: Praised lower fares and new entry through competition and removal of route/fare regulation, while retaining safety regulation and service guarantees for small communities.

sources.title: Depository Institutions Deregulation and Monetary Control Act
sources.evidence: Federal Reserve historian documents Carter signing deposit-interest deregulation while extending reserve requirements, deposit insurance and the Fed monetary-control framework.

sources.title: Presidential news conference: wage and price controls
sources.evidence: Carter rejected mandatory wage and price controls even under severe inflation, preferring voluntary restraint and federal example.

sources.title: Trade Agreements Act signing
sources.evidence: Backed Tokyo Round opening of trade, reciprocal removal of barriers, export opportunities and consumer savings; stressed fair trade and domestic prosperity.

sources.title: Sugar import fees proclamation signing
sources.evidence: Imposed sugar import fees to sustain domestic price-support operations: direct sectoral protection contrary to an absolute laissez-faire trade model.

sources.title: Prayer and the Civic Religion
sources.evidence: Explained his born-again Baptist faith and religious citizens influencing policy, while defending separation of church and state against government domination by religious organizations.

sources.title: Christian Post interview with Carter
sources.evidence: Personally opposed abortion except rape, incest or danger to maternal life while enforcing Roe; supported women religious leaders, accepted civil same-sex marriage and protected church autonomy; accepted modern science over literal cosmology.

sources.title: TEDWomen address
sources.evidence: Denounced female subordination, unequal pay, incarceration and executions. Supported the Swedish prostitution model penalizing buyers/pimps rather than exploited women. Recalled leaving Southern Baptist affiliation over subordination while continuing Sunday school.

sources.title: Who’s Afraid of Genetic Engineering?
sources.evidence: Strongly defended genetically engineered crops, medicines and vaccines against unsupported restrictions; said his own family farm used GM crops and productivity could reduce land clearing.

sources.title: Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act signing
sources.evidence: Protected extensive wilderness and native subsistence while explicitly allowing resource development in much of Alaska. Called for conservation, renewable energy, pesticide control and limits on environmental damage.

sources.title: Our Endangered Values: publisher record
sources.evidence: Publisher credits Jimmy Carter as author and reader; first publication 2005. Covers church/state separation, civil liberties, women, abortion, war, nuclear policy, science and environment.

sources.title: Nossos Valores em Risco: Brazilian Portuguese edition
sources.evidence: Bookseller identifies Brazilian Portuguese Manole edition, title Nossos Valores em Risco: A crise moral dos EUA, ISBN 9788520425138.

sources.title: Carter biography and bibliography
sources.evidence: Confirms life dates, presidency, deregulation and environmental record; lists Our Endangered Values (2005), Keeping Faith (1982) and Palestine Peace Not Apartheid (2006).

facts: 1979 education proposal: local/state primary responsibility with federal equal-opportunity support.
1978 tribal schooling statement preserved self-determination.
1979 Healthcare proposal unified fragmented state programs.
estrutura.tension: Cooperative constitutional federalism; national rights/service standards do not imply unitary local administration or secession.

facts: 2002 lecture defended democratic constitutional decisions and international election-related work.
2012 demanded judicial and congressional checks on detention.
representacao.tension: Representative democracy with rights checks, not unelected experts or replacement of elected institutions by assemblies.

facts: 1977 marijuana decriminalization was limited, not all-drug legalization.
2012 rejected warrantless surveillance and indefinite detention.
2015 opposed executions and supported penalizing sex buyers/pimps.
poder.tension: Strong civil liberties coexist with protective enforcement and public health; not unrestricted laissez-faire in private conduct.

facts: 1977 regularization plus employer sanctions and stronger borders.
1978 bilingual support aimed at English acquisition without suppressing first language.
imigracao.tension: Humanitarian pluralism and integration coexist with lawful-entry controls; neither cultural exclusion nor open borders.

facts: 2002 peace lecture prioritized UN consensus and diplomacy but defended readiness.
1980 Carter Doctrine reserved force in Persian Gulf.
2012 rejected targeted killings and abusive drone operations.
diplomacia.tension: Diplomacy first, credible defensive military, rejection of blanket abolition or unconditional pacifism.

facts: 1977–1981 conditioned aid on rights records.
1980 asserted vital Gulf interests.
2002 urged UN collective security and self-determination.
intervencao.tension: International engagement and sanctions remain compatible with opposition to unilateral domination; not isolationist or imperial nationalism.

facts: 1978 airline competition reforms preserved safety/public service obligations.
1979 health plan combined federal guarantee, private HMOs, employer insurance and fiscal staging.
economia.tension: Private productive economy with public guarantees; not nationalization of all strategic enterprises or wholly private basic services.

facts: 1978 opposed mandatory wage/price freezes.
1980 banking law deregulated rates while broadening monetary reserve rules.
1979 health plan included cost containment and competition.
controle.tension: Rejects both comprehensive state planning and unregulated markets; public goals and central banking persist.

facts: 1979 Act supported trade opening and international interdependence.
1978 sugar import fees explicitly protected a domestic support program.
comercio.tension: General trade liberalization with sectoral exceptions, not autarky or automatic zero tariffs.

facts: 1996 defended personal Baptist inspiration and church/state separation.
2012 defended independent religious congregations and equal civil marriage authority.
religiao.tension: Personal devotion is not theocracy; secular civil rules are not atheism or erasing public religious expression.

facts: 2012 accepted civil same-sex marriage but remained personally opposed to most abortion.
2015 advanced equality for women while supporting Swedish prostitution restrictions.
moral.tension: Equal rights and non-discrimination coexist with marital/sexual moral limits and protection of unborn life.

facts: 1998 forcefully endorsed GM crops and medical biotechnology.
1980 wilderness protection balanced limited resource development and conservation.
tecnologia.tension: Scientific pragmatism and stewardship; not anti-science naturalism or unlimited human enhancement.

uncertainties: Historical profile with preserved dual period, not a synthetic claim all later views were presidential policy. No need to infer current positions after his 2024 death.
Brazil-specific propositions are evaluated by corresponding institutional principle, not alleged Carter statements about contemporary Brazilian policies.

No direct statements verified on facial recognition, cryptocurrency, brain enhancement, cultivated meat, gender-neutral Portuguese or embryo intelligence selection. These are cautious analogical judgments using documented liberty, central-bank, science and moral positions; N only for genuine competing commitments.

UCSB and Carter Center speeches are primary Carter statements but not independent corroborating authors; State Department history, Federal Reserve historian and publisher/edition catalogs provide independent institutional checks.
Primary HuffPost 2015 marriage page failed to load. Independent 2012 Christian Post interview supplies direct civil-marriage support; no reliance on unavailable article.
